newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania privatisation body steps up sales.
newsitem.headline: Romania privatisation body steps up sales.

text.p: Romania's National Privatisation Agency (ANP) said on Tuesday it has drafted a four-year programme which includes incentives for foreign investors, to speed up delayed privatisations.
"Our draft includes legal initiatives and privatisation mechanisms for a faster property transfer to private hands," ANP president Valentin Ionescu told a news conference.

The programme, which has yet to be approved by the Reform Council, also envisages incentives for foreign investors, including foreign ownership of land and tax facilities -- seen as liable to boost a paltry $2.0 billion in foreign investment in the ex-communist country over the past seven years.
The move is in line with pledges by the centrist coalition which has been ruling Romania since last November's elections.
The new cabinet has promised to step up restructuring and the selloff of state firms, and to encourage foreign investment.
Privatisation mechanisms under the programme include public offerings and direct negotiations with potential investors, debt-for-equity swaps, and real estate leasing procedures.
Privatisation, a plank of market reforms launched after the 1989 end of communism, has been slow. It picked up slightly only with the 1995 launch of a mass selloff of 4,000 companies.
The State Ownership Fund (FPS), which has handled the bulk of privatisations since late 1992, acknowledged footdragging.

A FPS report released on Tuesday showed the main reasons behind the slow privatisation included domestic capital shortages, big payment arrears, an embryonic capital market and upsets in the banking system.
Payment arrears in Romania's economy are estimated at 22 trillion lei ($3.8 billion), almost the equivalent of the money supply.
So far, the FPS -- which started with some 6,500 companies in its portfortlio -- turned private some 3,000 companies.
"In terms of capital, these privatisations represent a scant 10 percent of an original 38 trillion lei," Ionescu said. -- Luli Popescu, Bucharest Newsroom 40-1 3120264 ($1=5738 Lei)
